meta.description: Not Galileo at his trial. The line’s earliest known printing is Giuseppe Baretti’s The Italian Library (1757), p. 52 — 124 years later.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'And yet it moves'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files ‘Eppur si muove’ under Galileo’s misattributed quotations. The 1757 page that first prints it gives no source at all.

answer.label: Not Galileo at his trial — first printed by Giuseppe Baretti in 1757
answer.authorDates: 1719–1789 · Italian critic, translator and lexicographer, long resident in London
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files Eppur si muove among Galileo’s misattributed quotations ↗ and names Giuseppe Baretti as apparently the first person to record the story. He did it in a short note on Galileo’s Dialogue in The Italian Library (London, 1757), p. 52 ↗: the moment he was set at liberty, Baretti writes, Galileo looked up to the sky, stamped his foot and said “Eppur si move.” No source is given for the anecdote, and the book was published 124 years after the 1633 trial it describes.

source.heading: The page the story starts on

docMeta.dd: Giuseppe Baretti (1719–1789), writing in English as Joseph Baretti
p. 52, in the entry on the 1632 Dialogue

source.excerpt: This is the celebrated Galileo, who was in the inquisition for six years, and put to the torture, for saying, that the earth moved. The moment he was set at liberty, he looked up to the sky and down to the ground, and, stamping with his foot, in a contemplative mood, said, Eppur si move; that is, still it moves, meaning the earth.
trail: Wikiquote lists the phrase under Galileo’s misattributed quotations ↗, notes that Giuseppe Baretti was apparently the first person to record the story, and cites Paul F. Boller and John George, They Never Said It: A Book of Fake Quotes, Misquotes, and Misleading Attributions (1990), p. 30.

We read Baretti’s page rather than a summary of it. The 1757 scan at the Internet Archive ↗ carries the sentence on p. 52, in italic, as Eppur si move — and carries no footnote, informant or date to support it.

Wikipedia’s article on the phrase ↗ records that the earliest biography of Galileo, written by his disciple Vincenzo Viviani in 1655–56, does not mention it, and that the records of his trial do not cite it.

Baretti’s framing does not survive contact with the record either. He has Galileo “in the inquisition for six years, and put to the torture”; Wikipedia’s account of the affair ↗ has him interrogated under the threat of torture, sentenced on 22 June 1633, and moved the following day to the house arrest he remained under for the rest of his life.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1757 scan, with the long ‘s’ modernised. Two details survive the transcription: the Italian is set as Eppur si move, not the muove spelling in circulation today, and “still it moves” is Baretti’s own English, not a later translator’s.

sourceLink.text: The Italian Library (1757), p. 52, at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The Italian Library was published in London in 1757 and is long out of copyright; the Internet Archive serves the complete scan ↗. Note that the four words at the top of this page are not the ones Baretti printed — he set the Italian Eppur si move and glossed it “still it moves.” “And yet it moves” is an unattributed literal rendering of a public-domain Italian phrase, so nothing here is anyone’s to license either.

author.name: Giuseppe Baretti
author.heading: About Giuseppe Baretti
author.metaLine: 1719–1789 · Italian literary critic, translator and lexicographer
author.bio: Giuseppe Marc’Antonio Baretti was born in Turin in 1719 and settled in London in 1751, where he taught Italian, compiled two influential English–Italian dictionaries, and became a fixture of Samuel Johnson’s circle alongside Reynolds, Garrick and Burke. He was a combative critic — his journal La Frusta letteraria was suppressed in Venice, and in 1769 he was tried for murder in London and acquitted on grounds of self-defence, with Johnson and Reynolds testifying to his character. The Italian Library (1757), the book that carries the Galileo anecdote, was his first notable work: a catalogue of Italian authors written to introduce them to English readers.

cite.sourceCitation: Giuseppe Baretti, The Italian Library. Containing An Account of the Lives and Works of the Most Valuable Authors of Italy (London: A. Millar, 1757), 52: “The moment he was set at liberty, he looked up to the sky and down to the ground, and, stamping with his foot, in a contemplative mood, said, Eppur si move; that is, still it moves, meaning the earth.” Earliest known appearance of the anecdote in print.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: It is the best closing line in the history of science, which is exactly the problem with it. Here is what the paper trail actually holds.

items.who: Galileo Galilei, muttering it at the Inquisition in 1633
items.why: The words appear in no work or letter of his and in no document of the trial, and his earliest biographer, Vincenzo Viviani, writing in 1655–56, does not mention them ↗. Saying it in that room would also have been an extraordinary risk to take moments after abjuring the belief it asserts.

Baretti prints the anecdote in a book of author biographies aimed at English readers, without naming an informant or a date ↗. That is 124 years after the trial — and it makes Baretti the earliest person known to have put the words in Galileo’s mouth, not necessarily the person who invented them.

items.scope: The painting that nearly settled it
items.who: A canvas dated 1643 or 1645, found in 1911
items.why: A picture acquired by the Belgian collector Jules van Belle showed Galileo in a cell with “E pur si muove” scratched on the wall ↗, seemingly putting the legend within a couple of years of his death. It was later found to be near-identical to a work of 1837; Wikimedia Commons catalogues that version as Eugène van Maldeghem’s, painted in 1837 and now in the Stedelijk Museum in Sint-Niklaas ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Wikiquote files it as misattributed ↗, and the earliest text anyone has produced is Baretti’s, 124 years after the fact. Galileo may well have thought it. Nobody has shown that he said it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: A recantation is a piece of theatre staged by the winning side, and this line is the audience refusing to accept the ending. Whoever first told it understood that the Earth’s motion is not a matter of opinion: the sentence works because the fact is indifferent to the verdict, and everyone in the room knew it.

That is also why it spread. Wikipedia notes that the book became widely published in Querelles Littéraires in 1761 ↗, and the phrase has been doing duty ever since as the shortest available argument that authority cannot legislate what is true — down to the same article’s note that Justice Antonin Scalia handed out an “E pur si muove” award to trial judges whose reversed opinions the Supreme Court later vindicated.
detailsBody: Baretti was not a historian of science. He was a critic and lexicographer who had moved to London in 1751, taught Italian, fell in with Samuel Johnson’s circle, and compiled The Italian Library as a guide to Italian authors for English readers ↗. The Galileo anecdote sits in that book as colour, one paragraph long, between a note on Tassoni and a remark that Galileo also wrote burlesque verse.

The words are not in dispute as words — they are in dispute as testimony. Galileo was sentenced on 22 June 1633 and confined for the rest of his life ↗, which ran until 8 January 1642, and he kept working through it: the Two New Sciences came out of that confinement in 1638. The defiance the phrase dramatises is real enough. Only the muttering is unattested.
context.pull: Printed for the first time 124 years after the trial it describes, with no source at all.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Galileo Galilei. The earliest known printing of the anecdote is Giuseppe Baretti's, in The Italian Library (1757); who first told the story is not established.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Eppur si muove" under Galileo Galilei’s Misattributed section, states that Giuseppe Baretti was apparently the first person to record the story, and cites Paul F. Boller and John George, They Never Said It (1990), p. 30.

Page 52 of Baretti’s The Italian Library (London: A. Millar, 1757) contains the sentence "The moment he was set at liberty, he looked up to the sky and down to the ground, and, stamping with his foot, in a contemplative mood, said, Eppur si move; that is, still it moves, meaning the earth," printed with no source or informant. Read from the page image and the OCR of the Internet Archive scan.
The Internet Archive holds the complete 1757 scan of Baretti’s The Italian Library, London: A. Millar.

Wikipedia’s article "And yet it moves" states that the earliest biography of Galileo, written by Vincenzo Viviani in 1655–1656, does not mention the phrase, that records of his trial do not cite it, that it was first reported in English print in 1757 by Baretti in The Italian Library, that the words were found in 1911 on a painting acquired by Jules van Belle of Roeselare dated 1643 or 1645, that the painting was later found to be nearly identical to one painted in 1837 by Eugene van Maldeghem, that the book was widely published in Querelles Litteraires in 1761, and that Justice Antonin Scalia gave an "E pur si muove" award to district judges whose overturned opinions the Supreme Court later vindicated.

Wikipedia’s "Galileo affair" states that Galileo was interrogated while threatened with physical torture, that the sentence of the Inquisition was issued on 22 June 1633, and that his formal imprisonment was commuted the following day to house arrest, which he remained under for the rest of his life.

Wikimedia Commons catalogues File:Galileo in prison.jpg as a painting by Eugene van Maldeghem, dated 1837, held at the Stedelijk Museum Sint-Niklaas, Belgium, showing Galileo with "E pur si muove" scratched on the cell wall.
Wikipedia gives Galileo Galilei’s dates as 15 February 1564 to 8 January 1642.

Wikipedia gives Giuseppe Marc’Antonio Baretti’s dates as 24 April 1719, Turin, to 5 May 1789, London, describes him as an Italian literary critic, poet, writer, translator and linguist who compiled two English-Italian dictionaries, notes his acquittal for murder on grounds of self-defence in 1769 with Johnson, Reynolds, Burke and Garrick testifying, and names The Italian Library (1757) as his first notable work.
